item.title: Misinformation about health and wellness can be convincing – here is how to spot it
item.description: Claims spread through trusted social networks when people share it because they want to help or warn others.
item.content:encoded:
Recent reports have highlighted AI-generated “doctors” spreading dubious health advice to millions of social media users. Fabricated wellness trends can travel just as quickly. A supposed “pink jelly” weight-loss treatment, for example, reportedly fooled at least one celebrity.

These examples gain credibility in different ways. Influencers can appear familiar and sincere, while AI-generated doctors can look like qualified professionals. Neither familiarity nor the appearance of expertise tells us whether a medical claim is accurate.

Turning to friends and family for health advice is understandable. They may know our circumstances in ways that a healthcare professional cannot during a brief appointment. They can provide emotional support and practical help, and their advice is usually well meant. But somebody can care about us, speak honestly and still be wrong.

Truth and trust

My own research and wider research on digital health misinformation shows that trust can play an important part in deciding which claims people accept. Trust in clinicians and scientific institutions is generally associated with lower susceptibility to false health claims. Misinformation can nevertheless spread through trusted social networks when people share it because they want to help or warn others.

item.title: ‘Recognised’ media outlets can report on courts, but not share audio, video clips of hearings: SC
item.description: The court issued a clarification on its July 24 interim order, saying that it should not be construed as a ‘blanket prohibition’.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court has clarified that its interim order restricting the sharing of audio and video recordings of court proceedings does not prevent “recognised news organisations” from reporting on hearings, Bar and Bench reported on Wednesday.

In its July 24 interim order, the court prohibited the extraction, editing, dissemination, reposting, uploading or monetisation of audio and video recordings of judicial proceedings on social media and other digital platforms without permission from the court authority.

A bench led by Chief Justice Surya Kant has clarified that the restriction should not be “construed as imposing a blanket prohibition on the reporting of court proceedings” but applies only to the use of audio and video recordings of hearings.

The interim order came on a public interest litigation filed by a journalist who has sought guidelines to regulate the clipping, editing, dissemination and monetisation of audiovisual recordings of court proceedings on digital platforms, Live Law reported.

The petition argues that the selective and decontextualised circulation of courtroom exchanges undermines the dignity of the courts and erodes public confidence in the justice system.

item.title: How the Iran-Pakistan ‘Axis of sympathy’ could reshape power in South Asia
item.description: This emerging alliance signals a huge geopolitical shift amid New Delhi’s tempered relations with Tehran.
item.content:encoded:
Last month, the Supreme Leader of Iran, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was buried in his hometown of Mashhad after a four-day ceremony. Many international delegations were present, but each country will have chosen their representatives with the utmost care. Sending high-ranking officials would go beyond mere diplomatic courtesy, and possibly signal an alliance.

Only two states sent their prime ministers to the funeral: Iraq and Pakistan, both of whom share a border with Iran. This decision indicates an emerging “Axis of Sympathy” between the countries, a new South-West Asian regional theatre that breaks the simple binaries of the Middle East and South Asia.

India – South Asia’s biggest power and Pakistan’s rival – sent a delegation that did not include Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Modi had also failed to condemn Khamenei’s assassination in a joint US-Israeli airstrike on February 28.

Indian network WIONews – owned by ZEE Media, India’s largest registered news network – gave the impression that Iran-India relations were in a good place. On 6 July 2026, the day of the funeral, one headline stated “‘Iranians will never forget’: Iran appreciates India’s participation in Khamenei funeral”.

item.title: If Vande Mataram is sung in madrasas, ‘heavens will not fall’, says Calcutta HC
item.description: The court made the verbal observation while hearing a PIL challenging the BJP government’s order making it mandatory to sing the patriotic song in the schools.
item.content:encoded:

The bench of Acting Chief Justice Tapabrata Chakraborty and Justice Partha Sarathi Sen was hearing a public interest litigation challenging a May 19 West Bengal government notification mandating that the song be sung in all madrasas under the state’s Minority Affairs and Madrasah Education Department.

The newly-formed Bharatiya Janata Party government has directed government model madrasas, recognised government-aided madrasas and recognised unaided madrasas to sing all six stanzas of the patriotic song.

During the hearing, Chakraborty remarked: “Heavens will not fall...today if I am asked to utter a quote that is not in my religion...what will happen? I will become a person not belonging to that religion?”

item.title: ‘Another drop of hope in flow’: Poems that grapple with the reality of an imperfect world
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Cries’, by Soumya Mukerji.
item.content:encoded:
Fani

a storm
like us
raging
like us
ruthless
like us
circling
like us
rising
like us
spiralling
like us
tiring
like us
repenting
like us
wearying
like us
relenting
unlike us.

[Written while travelling to the ancient village of Gohaldia in the hinterland of Odisha, India, which was recovering from the ruthless cyclone, Fani, in 2019. The cyclone displaced more than a million people in the state as a result of the indiscriminate destruction of natural

ecosystems. A visit to Mayurbhanj that year was almost a beckoning of my own ancestral history, deeply intertwined with that of Odisha’s from a time of the Bengal Renaissance. It was during this journey that I witnessed the aftermath of the cyclone – and, more importantly, the resilience of the region’s people, hard at work.]


No cure but poetry is sure

what if I told you a poem was stronger?
what if I told you a poem fought longer?

the poem worked from away and worked from home
on burning lands, bursting seas

debilitating injury and disease
a para’s cetamol
rhyma moclobemide
sane-itiser
prose-thetics

healing the cursed
aiding the nursed
a spell four thousand years old
with the universe in its fold

it’ll fix this anxious, cold you

a poem in quarantine
a poem in a glass of wine

enough to cure a species diseased
enough to resurrect a humanity deceased.

Speaking to reporters in Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, he said the decision was taken because “what India needs right now is a pressure group”.

Pressure groups are viewed as formal or informal organisations that seek to influence government policies and decisions without contesting elections. They can act as a bridge between citizens and the government.

Ahead of a meeting of the core members of the CJP, Dipke said on Wednesday that the protests held in Delhi against alleged mismanagement of competitive examinations showed the citizens’ dwindling trust in “the political system, the judiciary, the media or the Election Commission”.

In view of this, the CJP would hold discussions about the government’s Ethanol Blended Petrol programme and rising unemployment in the future, PTI quoted Dipke as saying.

“The support that our movement received was not limited to education,” he said. “That is why we believe that, to restore accountability and neutrality in these institutions, a public movement and public pressure are needed.”

“We need to tread carefully so that these youngsters do not indulge in violence,” said Chief Justice Surya Kant while hearing a petition by retired Air Force officers seeking action against the organisers of the protests that spread across the country in July.

Kant added: “The better course is to counsel them and pacify them. The most powerful tool is listening. Listen to them and understand why they are shouting.”

item.title: Podcast: What today’s engineers can learn from a technocrat of colonial India
item.description: Writer Aparajith Ramnath details M Visvesvaraya’s achievements but also offers some cautionary words about technocratic thinking.
item.content:encoded:
Engineers rarely become celebrities. Yet M Visvesvaraya (1861-1962) is a notable exception, a man whose career and achievements continue to be widely celebrated in India. He presided over the construction of some of colonial India’s most audacious development projects, such as the Krishnarajasagara dam and reservoir near Mysuru. He became an evangelist for industrialisation and set out a technocratic vision for an independent India.

That vision remains powerful today. Aparajith Ramnath, the author of Engineering a Nation and winner of the 2025 Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay NIF Book Prize, has provided Visvesvaraya with the comprehensive biography he has long deserved. In this episode of Past Imperfect, Ramnath details Visvesvaraya’s achievements but also offers some cautionary words about technocratic thinking.

Born in a small town in the erstwhile princely state of Mysore, Visvesvaraya went on to have multiple careers. In 1884, he joined the Bombay Public Works Department as a civil engineer, entering a profession where a solid glass ceiling remained intact for Indians. He nevertheless rose through the ranks with stunning speed. Leaving Bombay, he accepted the position of chief engineer of Mysore state and, in 1912, became the state’s diwan or prime minister. item.description: The state is expecting another spell of intense rainfall by the weekend.
item.content:encoded:
The toll in rain-related incidents in Kerala has risen to 25 in the past six days, The Hindu reported on Wednesday. Four persons were missing.

The state has been receiving heavy and incessant rainfall since Friday, triggering flash floods and landslides.

While rainfall had reduced, the state was expecting another spell of intense rain by the weekend because of a low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal, the newspaper reported.

The India Meteorological Department has forecast heavy rainfall in parts of central Travancore region, including Ernakulam, Idukki and parts of Kottayam, and in the northern districts of Kozhikode, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod, the newspaper reported.

The rest of the state is likely to receive above-normal rainfall, except Thiruvananthapuram and parts of Kollam.

The state has set up 418 relief camps to shelter more than 18,400 persons, The Hindu reported.

item.title: Maharashtra bans analogue paneer for a year
item.description: Citing public health concerns, the order barred the retail sale of the product, and prohibited restaurants and caterers from using or serving it.
item.content:encoded:
Maharashtra has banned the production and sale of analogue paneer for a year.

The order also bars restaurants, caterers and cloud kitchens from preparing, using and serving analogue paneer.

A gazette order issued by the commissioner of the state’s Food and Drug Administration on July 30 cited public health concerns to impose the ban.

Analogue paneer is a non-dairy or a partially synthetic substitute for paneer. It replaces milk fat and milk solids with cheaper vegetable oils, making the dairy products cheaper.

The food and drug authority cited a 2016 Supreme Court order as having directed the Centre and state governments to implement the 2006 Food Safety and Standards Act more effectively. The court directions have cast a continuing obligation upon the authority to take effective preventive measures against the adulteration of milk and dairy products, it said.

The gazette order said that the food and drug administration’s Central Advisory Committee set up in October had recorded that no quality parameters had been defined for analogue in the context of dairy. In absence of the standards, analogue paneer was “essentially a sub-standard product” that “only increases deliberate adulteration”, it added.

He warned that the passage of the draft legislation could hurt relations between Washington and New Delhi.

Registration under the Act is mandatory for a non-profit organisation to receive foreign funds.

“Christians have been in India since St Thomas the Apostle travelled to the Malabar Coast just decades after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Moore said on social media.

Despite this long history, India’s Parliament is considering amending the rules “to permit government takeovers of churches and religious charities”, he added.

“This is a clear attack against Christians,” said the Republican representative from West Virginia. “If this bill proceeds in this way, it would be a point of major concern in our bilateral relationship with India.”

item.title: RBI keeps repo rate unchanged at 5.25%
item.description: The impact of the El Niño weather phenomenon on rainfall distribution remains a risk, the central bank said.
item.content:encoded:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Monetary Policy Committee on Wednesday kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%.

The repo rate is the interest rate at which the central bank lends money to commercial banks. The Monetary Policy Committee reviews the rate every two months.

The committee had cut the repo rate by 25 basis points from 5.50% in December and kept it unchanged in February, April and June.

A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Basis points are used to describe the percentage change in the value of a financial instrument.

Central banks usually reduce repo rates to stimulate economic growth by making borrowing cheaper for individuals and businesses. This translates to lower equated monthly instalments for borrowers.

On Wednesday, the policy committee said that it had decided to maintain its monetary policy stance as “neutral”.

A neutral stance means that the Reserve Bank remained flexible in adjusting policy rates based on prevailing economic conditions.

State of the economy

The consumer price index inflation increased to 4.4% in June mainly because of higher food and fuel inflation, the Reserve Bank said. item.description: The Election Commission said that the voter card issued to Rafikul Biswas during the special intensive revision of West Bengal’s electoral rolls was genuine.
item.content:encoded:

item.title: When you hit ‘delete’, what really happens to your data?
item.description: There is a pressing need for provision of concise, accessible and clear information about how deletion really works.
item.content:encoded:
Deletion is a common part of modern life. We send files and folders to the recycle bin all the time, and often get rid of unwanted personal accounts. But do you know what really happens when you hit the “delete” button?

The process of deletion is often poorly explained by tech providers. Lack of transparency around how requests are processed, and the absence of clear confirmation that data has been removed, are frequently highlighted in research.

These issues are not limited to operating systems. On social media platforms and a wide range of subscription services, deletion mechanisms are often just as unclear. Such misconceptions can have serious implications for the wellbeing of users, exposing them to security and privacy vulnerabilities.

A further complication is that many users fear losing data, files, photos and videos through accidental deletion – a condition dubbed “diagraphephobia”. Though this is not a recognised pathology, studies of digital hoarding behaviour show that some people get very anxious at the thought of losing or accidentally deleting personal information such as photos and music.

Such concerns extend the amount of personal data that sits untended but undeleted, ready for potential misappropriation.

It was formally described in 1956 by H Khajuria of the Zoological Survey of India and named Presbytis geei in honour of Gee.

The golden langur is a medium-sized primate. Males weigh 10-12 kg and females 9.5-10 kg. They are less sexually dimorphic than other colobines such as grey langurs (Semnopithecus spp). item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Monday verbally clarified to the Union government that the 2026 amendments to the Transgender Persons Protection of Rights Act will not retrospectively or by default invalidate transgender cards issued to members of the community under the previous legislation, The Hindu reported.

The amendments to the 2019 Act, cleared by Parliament in March, redefine who qualifies as a transgender person. They remove transgender persons’ right to a self-perceived gender identity. They also limit the scope of the law to those with certain biological or physiological characteristics, intersex variations, or specific socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta.

The law makes medical evaluation and certification mandatory for legal gender recognition. It underlines that the authority to permit such transitions is vested in medical professionals operating under a medical board.

On Monday, petitioners against the amendments, who include members of the transgender community and activists, contended that the amendments give the government complete power to determine gender identity, The Hindu reported. item.title: Bali’s fishing canoes are vanishing as tourism changes Indonesia’s coastline
item.description: The traditional boats with colourful carvings of the mythical elephant-fish on their prows represent centuries of maritime heritage.
item.content:encoded:
Five decades ago, Bali’s coastline was adorned with traditional fishing canoes with colourful carvings of mythical elephant-fish. Where did they go?

The disappearance of these canoes tells a much bigger story about how tourism, collecting and coastal change are reshaping Indonesia’s living maritime heritage – and why preserving these traditions matters.

The boats that once lined Bali’s beaches

Before Bali became one of the worlds’ most popular tourist destinations, fishing villages lined the beaches of Benoa, Nusa Dua and Sanur, along the island’s southern coast.

Generations of fishers built and sailed jukung pelasan – traditional timber double-outrigger sailing canoes with colourful carved gajah mina (elephant-fish) prows.

The gajah mina is a creature in Balinese Hindu tradition with the head of an elephant and the body of a fish. Symbolising unity and harmony between land and sea, it is said to protect crews during voyages and provide safe passage.

These were not just fishing boats; they were central to daily life in southern Bali.

The jukung were symbols of status and community identity. They embodied generations of craftsmanship, spiritual belief and maritime knowledge. They expressed the economic, social and spiritual life of Bali’s coastal communities, and reflected the enduring relationship between its people and the sea.

Today, however, only a handful remain.

Modi was repeating a line that Indian prime ministers have recited for decades. It is a comfortable formulation that costs New Delhi nothing and offends no one.

A week later, Indian officials at the Palestine Donor Group meetings in Brussels reiterated the commitment, welcoming diplomatic avenues towards Palestinian statehood and UN membership.

But this language now describes a country that no longer exists in any coherent, contiguous form, and every week that passes widens the gap between rhetoric and reality.

With Vikram commencing his army career in distant Sopore, I want to digress a bit and introspect on the dynamics in Palampur that shaped both his ambition and prowess, enabling him to sustain himself physically and mentally in the extraordinarily challenging mission that he was about to embark upon as an armyman. And one of the key contributors in this journey of grit and strength was his competence in sports.

In fact, both Vikram and I were very keen sportspersons. From an early age, we became proficient in playing table tennis, which along with cricket, was a very popular sport in Palampur those days. item.title: How Shakespeare’s ‘The Tempest’ can help readers understand the hidden costs of AI
item.description: The play offers a useful means of understanding how power operates through hidden infrastructures.
item.content:encoded:
In the 400 years since his death, William Shakespeare’s work has been used as a lens through which to interpret countless developments he could never have anticipated – from modern psychology and political theory to colonialism and climate change. His writing possesses an uncanny ability to illuminate nearly every facet of the human condition.

Yet, as a decolonial scholar and an AI researcher, we believe that Shakespeare’s plays are now beginning to illuminate something beyond that as well – the emergent forms of artificial intelligence that increasingly shape and challenge our understanding of what it means to think, act and be.

AI tools have rapidly become part of many people’s everyday lives. Yet relatively few probably consider the physical infrastructure that makes these systems possible. Each prompt we send is processed in distant data centres: vast facilities that generate responses by predicting the most likely sequence of words based on patterns learned from enormous datasets.

This dynamic of distant, unseen control recalls Shakespeare’s The Tempest, a play that offers a useful means of understanding how power operates through hidden infrastructures.

Two of Georges Perec’s French novellas have been brought together in Things: A Story of the Sixties with A Man Asleep – translations into English of Les Choses (1965) and Un homme qui dort (1967). They have been translated by David Bellos and Andrew Leak, respectively. Things was a runaway hit in French, making it to readers’ bookshelves as well as becoming prescribed reading at universities. item.title: Remembering Janabai, the Bahujan woman who promoted maternal care and education in colonial Bombay
item.description: Her life story challenges ideas about male-dominated social reform movements in India.
item.content:encoded:
In South Mumbai’s Mandvi Koliwada sits a terracotta-colored building bearing the name Janabai and Madhavrao Rokade Municipal School.

As is the case with public buildings in many Indian cities, the names of the personalities that adorn them are often unfamiliar. Some of them are linked to relatively recent politicians and cultural figures. A few of them have a deeper historical connection. The Rokade municipal school falls in the second category.

The school was established in 1879, making it one of Mumbai’s earliest modern schools. It was started by Madhavrao Rokade.

For anyone interested in Mumbai’s socio-political history from this period, Madhavrao Rokade is remembered as a key member and writer associated with the Satyashodhak movement. This was a movement started by Jotirao and Savitribai Phule in Pune in 1873 to confront the upper-caste dominance in everyday life and to work toward inculcating a sense of collective consciousness among Bahujan communities, especially through education.

Rokade contributed to this movement by starting and running this school for many years with limited support. He was also known for his periodic writings in the late 19th century in newspapers such as Dinbandhu (Brother of the Oppressed) and Shetkaryacha Kaivari (Protector of Farmers).

It’s the 13th century, and Delhi is slowly slipping into decline under the ageing Sultan Alauddin Khilji. Fears of famine, foreign invasion and court intrigue plague the city. In the midst of all this ferment, a strange, enigmatic object appears in the sky. No one knows what it is, but the persistence of the apparition and its passivity seem to portend something sinister.

The Sultan orders Amir Hassan al-Shirazi – Sufi, poet, intellectual and, some would say, the Sultan’s favourite – to investigate this cosmic phenomenon. Hassan’s search takes him to every quarter of Delhi, and everywhere, paranoia, confusion and fear reign supreme. Just when it seems that the city will collapse under the weight of its own misgivings, a distant grey cloud approaches. As its people watch, awestruck, strange creatures – half-man, half-bird – descend on the city. It is a takeover by the Avians and the death of the old order in Delhi.

item.title: Why the philosophical conversations in Mohammad Iqbal’s poetry are relevant to modern political life
item.description: Iqbal transformed poetry into a forum of civilisational inquiry, where god, humanity, revolution, religion and power converse with one another.
item.content:encoded:
Raza Mir’s introduction to Mohammad Iqbal’s poetry and philosophical work, along with some biographical reflection in Iqbal: Poet of the East, provides extensive knowledge to the beginner who wants to read Iqbal’s philosophical work regarding the concepts of Khudhi, Shaheen and Socialism. The introductory book also familiarises readers with the intricate threads of Iqbal’s engagement with socialist thinkers such as Karl Marx and Vladimir Lenin. Yet, beyond a limited intellectual circle, many continue to reduce Iqbal to selective ideological readings, overlooking his poetic invocations of Hindu deities and civilisational hymns.


Mohammad Iqbal has been almost imprisoned in the image of a flamboyant poet of Saare Jahaan Se Acha or as an ideologue of Pakistan, conceiving him as a political and religious figure while ignoring his body of philosophical work. However, he participated actively in the pre-independent Indian politics, offered his opinion on partition, and wrote several patriotic pieces in Urdu, including Tarana-e-Hindi. Ironically, Iqbal is one of the most quoted and least read figures of the subcontinent, which has created a fragmented image of the poet-philosopher. Nationalists invoke him selectively, Islamists claim him exclusively, while secular critics often dismiss him. Such selective appropriations have reduced a restless intellectual to an ideological emblem.

item.title: How lab-grown diamonds have changed the game
item.description: The saying goes that ‘diamonds are forever’. But what if the market for them isn’t?
item.content:encoded:
You’ve probably heard the saying “a diamond is forever”. What if the market for them – with its hefty price tags – isn’t?

Back in March, Rio Tinto ended production at its Diavik diamond mine in Canada after 23 years. Earlier this month, diamond mining company De Beers announced a two-year production pause at the company’s flagship Venetia mine in South Africa.

De Beers is majority-owned by global mining giant Anglo American. According to a Bloomberg report this week, Anglo is now in talks to sell its 85% stake for about US$1 billion – a tiny fraction of the US$18 billion it was valued at when taken private in 2001.

So, what’s going on? The industry certainly hasn’t run out of diamonds to mine. But current prices and costs have made continued production of natural diamonds harder to justify.

item.title: Who was Homer, author of the ‘Odyssey’?
item.description: When the ‘Odyssey’ first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.
item.content:encoded:
Who wrote the Odyssey?

Homer, obviously: that is what we’ve been told since the late 6th century BCE, when ancient Greeks started crediting the Odyssey to a blind bard from the rocky isle of Chios.

But this “Homer” appeared at least a century later than the poem itself. When the Odyssey first began to circulate in ancient Greece, no one knew its author. The song seems to have created the singer, not the other way around.

How can you have a poem without a poet? Two American researchers, Milman Parry and Albert Lord, came across a possible answer.

In the 1930s, Parry and Lord travelled to the Balkans to study still-living traditions of epic poetry. In Yugoslavia and Albania, they found bards who sang of heroes from long ago. These singers did not recite from a book. Most of them couldn’t read or write at all. Instead, they improvised their epics as they sang. They knew the story by heart, but told it in different words with each performance.

Balkan bards achieved this by relying on a stock of formulaic scenes, lines and phrases, which they combined on the spot. The formulae were passed down from teacher to student, so that all singers tended to sound alike.

item.title: Can fuel-reliant South Asia survive the next global conflict?

Amid signs that the US and Iran have paused their latest round of hostilities, it is time to examine the economies that the conflict effectively brought to a standstill this year.

In March 2026, when the exchange of threats and missiles choked the Strait of Hormuz, the bill landed on the doors of Dhaka, Islamabad and Colombo long before it reached Washington or Brussels.

The moment revealed itself less as a geopolitical crisis and more as unending queues for fuel in South Asia, with restaurants shuttered and households plunged into darkness by relentless load shedding.

Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka – three countries with virtually no domestic oil reserves and no meaningful influence over global commodity prices – absorbed energy shocks for a war they did not cause. item.title: ‘The Business of Business Is Not Just Business’: A changing view of Indian corporate responsibility

The title of Sutapa Banerjee’s edited volume, The Business of Business Is (Not) Just Business, underlines something that few would argue against. The era when businesses could legitimately argue that the only responsibility they have is to their shareholders is behind us. The role of business is widely acknowledged to encompass a much larger range of stakeholders. Businesses are not exempt from society; they play an active role in shaping it not just in economic terms but also culturally. Employment, migration, gender, environment, aspirations, access to opportunity, public discourse and the very idea of progress are all shaped in some way or the other by business.

DD Kosambi: One Life Many Worlds, Ram Ramaswamy

Historian. Mathematician. Marxist. Polymath. DD Kosambi defied labels. The range and intellectual heft of his scholarship was truly astounding, with fundamental contributions in differential geometry and analyses in mathematics, the Kosambi distance in genetics, a statistical analysis of ancient coin hoards, a radical reinterpretation of Indian history and stellar compilations of the poetry of Vidyakara and Bhartrhari-all this in addition to a firm commitment to world peace and environmental activism.

Yet, for a man who contributed so much to the Indian intellectual tradition, he remains largely unknown. Sixty years after his passing, there is scant recognition of his talents-he is quoted more often than he is read and praised more often than he is analysed.

Ram Ramaswamy’s biography of Kosambi seeks to correct this lapse. Set against the backdrop of fascinating social, political, scientific and historiographical transformation in the subcontinent, and drawing from letters, journal entries, family accounts and unprecedented archival material, DD Kosambi: One Life, Many Worlds reveals a rare incandescent genius and a fearless independent spirit with boundless curiosity-whose relevance in the fields of pedagogy, research and invention can be seen even today.
